analysis.one_liner: Allows the FDA to approve cheaper copies of expensive brand-name biologic drugs.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 35 cosponsors, including 8 Republicans, but never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: Biologic drugs are made from living cells and are among the most expensive medicines; no cheaper copies could be approved under the law as written. This bill would have created an FDA pathway to approve copies shown to be 'comparable' or 'interchangeable' with the brand product, opened the door to substitution with cheaper versions, set review deadlines, and laid out how patent disputes between the brand maker and the copy maker would be resolved. The bill was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients taking expensive biologic drugs, who would gain access to cheaper FDA-approved copies once the underlying patents were addressed; generic drug manufacturers, who would gain a new market; and payers including employers and government programs, who would bear lower drug costs.

how_it_helps.text: Creates an abbreviated FDA approval pathway for 'comparable' and 'interchangeable' biological products, allowing copies to rely on data showing they match the brand product rather than repeating the full clinical testing the brand performed.

Requires the Secretary to determine whether a copy is 'interchangeable' — meaning it can be expected to produce the same clinical result in any given patient — which is the determination that allows substitution.

Sets firm review deadlines (final action within 8 months of submission or 180 days after filing acceptance, whichever is earlier) and limits the ability of outside parties to delay approval through petitions.

Grants the first interchangeable copy a bounded exclusivity period (as short as 180 days after first marketing, or one year after approval if the copy maker is not sued) to reward the first company to bring a copy to market.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name biologic drug manufacturers, whose monopoly-priced products would face copy competition, and whose patents could be challenged under a streamlined dispute process that in some cases limits remedies to a reasonable royalty.

drawbacks.text: Approval of a copy would rest on demonstrating 'comparability' and 'highly similar' structure rather than an identical molecule; biologics are complex products made in living cells, so abbreviated evidence carries a trade-off between faster, cheaper approval and the depth of clinical proof behind each copy.

The bill grants the first interchangeable copy its own exclusivity window — up to 36 months if litigation is ongoing — during which the FDA must defer interchangeability determinations for later copies, postponing full competition.

The patent provisions limit brand makers' remedies in some circumstances to a reasonable royalty and bar suits on patents not disclosed in response to the copy maker's information request, reducing the leverage patent holders otherwise have to keep a copy off the market.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit — cheaper versions of some of the most expensive drugs on the market — is large, but it depends on copy makers actually succeeding in the new approval process and on the patent-dispute mechanism working without endless litigation. The exclusivity for the first interchangeable copy is a deliberate speed bump, trading some competition for an incentive to be first. The safety trade-off from abbreviated evidence is real but was paired with postmarketing study requirements. On balance the design is reasonable for its purpose; the bill's problem was not its drafting but that it never moved.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to two House committees the day it was introduced, the bill sat at the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee for the rest of the Congress and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman introduced the bill on February 14, 2007, with four original cosponsors including Republican Rep. Jo Ann Emerson of Missouri.
The bill attracted 35 cosponsors, 27 Democrats and 8 Republicans.
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction, and referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee the next day.
No further action was taken for the remainder of the 110th Congress, which ended January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name biologic manufacturers, who kept exclusive markets and brand-level pricing with no copy competition for the remainder of the Congress; patients continued paying brand prices.

for.name: Rep. Henry Waxman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 35 cosponsors.

for.name: 35 House cosponsors (27 Democrats, 8 Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsor Rep. Jo Ann Emerson (R-MO).

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill out of the Health Subcommittee for a hearing or markup during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Brand-name biologic drug industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed early biosimilar legislation, which would have opened its most profitable products to copy competition.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan — 35 members including 8 Republicans and original cosponsor Jo Ann Emerson of Missouri — and no vote was ever held to reveal a partisan split.

industries.note: Biologics are among the highest-priced drugs, protected by monopoly because no approval pathway for copies existed. The bill would let copy makers challenge patents and win approval with less clinical data, eroding that pricing power — which is why the industry's interest ran against the bill that would have lowered patients' costs.
The bill creates a new market for copy makers, with a bounded exclusivity reward for the first interchangeable product. Their gain comes directly from prices falling for patients.
